data-analyst.intro: Learn to turn raw data into decisions. From collecting and cleaning to visualising and presenting — the skills every business, government, and NGO needs.

skillDomains.name: Data Collection
skillDomains.description: Where data comes from, how to structure it, and how to avoid bias.

skills.name: Data Sources
skills.description: Identify where data lives and how to get it.

modules.title: Where data comes from
modules.content:
Data in West Africa comes from more places than most people think:

  • Surveys — the most common in NGO and government work
  • Mobile money transaction logs — huge and continuous
  • Mobile phone metadata — anonymised, aggregated
  • Market records — often on paper, needing digitisation
  • Government registries — births, businesses, land
  • Sensors — weather, agriculture, traffic (growing fast)

Your first job is always the same: find where the data is, understand its limits, and know what you can't do with it.

modules.title: Structured vs unstructured
modules.content:
Structured data

Organised into rows and columns. Easy to analyse. Examples: a spreadsheet of sales, a database of patients.

Semi-structured

Some organisation, but not tabular. Examples: JSON files, emails with metadata.

Unstructured

No fixed format. Examples: WhatsApp messages, voice notes, photos, handwritten receipts.

In West Africa, most real data is unstructured or semi-structured. Learning to convert it into something analysable is a critical skill.

steps.q: A spreadsheet of student grades — which type?
A folder of photos of receipts — which type?
steps.f: Images are unstructured. They need OCR or manual digitisation to analyse.

steps.q: A JSON response from a mobile money API — which type?
steps.f: JSON has structure but isn't tabular. Semi-structured.

skillDomains.name: Analysis
skillDomains.description: Turn raw numbers into insight. Averages, trends, and comparison.

skills.name: Descriptive Statistics
skills.description: Summarise a dataset with the right numbers.

modules.title: Mean, median, mode
modules.content:
Mean

Add everything, divide by count. Good for symmetric data. Bad when outliers exist.

Median

The middle value when sorted. Good when outliers exist.

Mode

The most frequent value. Good for categories.

Example

Salaries: 20k, 22k, 25k, 30k, 500k. Mean = 119.4k (misleading). Median = 25k (accurate).

Always ask: is this data symmetric? If not, use the median.

steps.q: Incomes of 100 households, one is a millionaire. Which measure best describes typical income?
steps.f: The millionaire skews the mean. Median reflects typical experience.

steps.q: Most common occupation in a district. Which measure?
steps.f: Categories use mode. "Farmer" can't be averaged.

steps.q: Scores on a test with a few very low outliers. Which measure for central tendency?
steps.f: Median is more robust when outliers exist.

skills.name: Data Cleaning
skills.description: Real data is messy. Cleaning is 70% of the job.

modules.title: Why cleaning is the job
modules.content:
Data analysts spend roughly 70% of their time cleaning data, not analysing it. This surprises everyone who starts.

Common problems

  • Missing values
  • Duplicates
  • Inconsistent formats (dates as text, numbers as strings)
  • Typos in category names ("male", "Male", "M", "man")
  • Outliers that may or may not be errors
  • Encoding issues (accents mangled)

A clean dataset is worth more than a clever analysis on a dirty one.

steps.q: A gender column has values: male, Male, M, m, man, female, F, Woman. What do you do?
steps.f: Standardise into a consistent format. Never delete data you can fix.

steps.q: A date column has values like "12/03/2024", "March 12 2024", "2024-03-12". What do you do?
steps.f: ISO format is unambiguous. Convert everything to it.

steps.q: A salary column has one value of 999999999 which is clearly an error. What do you do?
o: Investigate before deciding, then handle transparently
steps.f: Investigate first. Then document what you did and why. Never silently change data.

skillDomains.name: Visualisation
skillDomains.description: Communicate insight through charts and dashboards.

modules.title: Chart types and their jobs
modules.content:
Bar chart

Comparing categories. "Sales by region."

Line chart

Change over time. "Monthly revenue."

Pie chart

Parts of a whole. Use sparingly — hard to read with many slices.

Scatter plot

Relationship between two variables. "Price vs quantity sold."

Histogram

Distribution of one variable. "Distribution of ages."

Bad chart choice makes good data useless. Choose based on the question, not the style.

steps.q: You want to show how malaria cases changed month by month over a year.
You want to compare average income across 5 countries.
You want to show the relationship between rainfall and crop yield.

skills.name: Answering Stakeholder Questions
skills.description: Understand what decision your analysis supports.

modules.title: Start with the decision
modules.content:
Before you touch data, ask: what decision does this support?

Examples:

  • A shop owner deciding which product to restock → analysis of sales velocity and margins
  • An NGO deciding where to open a clinic → analysis of population density and travel times
  • A bank deciding loan criteria → analysis of default patterns

Analysis without a decision is a hobby. Analysis in service of a decision is a career.

skillDomains.name: Tools
skillDomains.description: The software you'll use every day.

skills.name: Spreadsheets
skills.description: Excel, Google Sheets — still the most-used analytics tool in the world.

modules.title: Why spreadsheets still matter
modules.content:
AI and Python get the headlines. But 80% of real analysis in West African businesses, NGOs, and government happens in spreadsheets.

What to master

  • Sorting and filtering
  • SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MIN, MAX
  • IF and IFERROR
  • VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP (joining datasets)
  • Pivot tables (summary tables in seconds)
  • Charts

If you can do these six things well, you can get hired.

steps.q: You want the total of column B for rows 2-100.
steps.f: SUM adds values. COUNT counts them.

steps.q: You want to show "Pass" if score ≥50 and "Fail" otherwise.
steps.f: IF with a condition and two outcomes.

steps.q: You have two tables and want to pull a value from one into the other by matching an ID.
steps.f: VLOOKUP (or XLOOKUP in newer tools) joins data by matching keys.

skills.name: SQL Basics
skills.description: Query databases directly — the next step after spreadsheets.

modules.title: What SQL is for
modules.content:
Spreadsheets top out at ~100,000 rows. Databases handle billions. SQL (Structured Query Language) is how you talk to them.

The four commands you'll use most

  • SELECT — pick columns
  • FROM — pick the table
  • WHERE — filter rows
  • GROUP BY — aggregate

Example: SELECT region, SUM(sales) FROM transactions WHERE year = 2024 GROUP BY region

That single query does what 20 spreadsheet steps would.
